claim: The Israeli right is like American Republicans and the Israeli left is like Democrats.

heard.who: Bernard Avishai, writer, in The New Yorker, 2016
heard.quote: The Israeli left, like American Democrats, has assumed that the poorest voters could be appealed to as a class with social-democratic promises.

heard.who: Bernard Avishai, writer, in The New Yorker, 2016
heard.quote: During the Obama Administration, Likud became an ally of the Republicans.

answer: In Israel, the Israel Democracy Institute and other sources describe left and right as defined mainly by one's stance on the conflict (territory, a Palestinian state, security), with religion and state a second line of division and small differences between the camps on economic issues. In America the parties divide across many issues: government, economy, immigration, race, abortion. The Institute's 2022 index says the Israeli divide is now more reminiscent of Democrats against Republicans, across a range of issues. Pew's 2025 Israeli survey found 54% of the left, 29% of the centre and 7% of the right saying a way can be found for Israel and a Palestinian state to coexist; Gallup's 2025 US survey, asking a different question, found 76% of Democrats and 41% of Republicans favouring an independent Palestinian state.

facts.text: Scholars and commentators describe the Israeli left-right axis as mainly about the conflict with the Palestinians: territory, a Palestinian state, settlements and security.

sources.title: Doves and Hawks in Israeli Society: Stances on National Security
sources.quote: The division between political left and right is primarily dependant on opinions regarding national security, and especially the question of the territories.

sources.title: What 'right' and 'left' mean in Israel today
sources.quote: In Israel, the left-right divide is shaped less by economics than by positions on Palestinian statehood, occupation and Jewish sovereignty.

sources.title: The ideas of Israel
sources.quote: we therefore use the left-right spectrum in line with the Israeli understanding that it is determined by one's security stance, especially regarding the Palestinians.

sources.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022
sources.quote: whereas in the past it was crystal clear what Right and Left meant, since the distinction was based mainly on opinions about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict

facts.text: The Israel Democracy Institute's Israeli Democracy Index 2022 says that, whereas Right and Left once meant mainly opinions about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, today the division between the two camps is more reminiscent of that between the Democrats and the Republicans in the United States, reflecting two opposing sets of opinions on a range of issues; the writer Bernard Avishai drew a parallel between the Israeli left and American Democrats in The New Yorker in 2016.

sources.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022
sources.quote: whereas in the past it was crystal clear what Right and Left meant, since the distinction was based mainly on opinions about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict

sources.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022
sources.quote: today the division between the two camps is more reminiscent of that between the Democrats and the Republicans in the United States.

sources.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022
sources.quote: it reflects two opposing sets of opinions, emotions, and behaviors that apply to a range of issues, from what Zionism means today, questions of religion and state, and Jewish versus universal values

sources.publisher: The New Yorker (Bernard Avishai, 2016; a writer's opinion, not a reader of the IDI record)
sources.title: What Americans Against Trump Can Learn from the Failures of the Israeli Opposition
sources.quote: The Israeli left, like American Democrats, has assumed that the poorest voters could be appealed to as a class with social-democratic promises.

facts.text: Religion and state is a second line of division, but it does not line up neatly with left and right: ultra-Orthodox voters sit furthest right on religion in public life yet are more centrist on the conflict.

sources.title: Israel's Religiously Divided Society
sources.quote: on some issues, including those pertaining to religion in public life, there is a clear overlap: haredim are furthest to the right and hilonim are furthest to the left

sources.title: United Torah Judaism
sources.quote: regarding foreign policy and security, United Torah Judaism is a centrist party, which determines its positions based on religious concerns more than security concerns or diplomatic considerations.

sources.title: What 'right' and 'left' mean in Israel today
sources.quote: Coalition choices are driven less by a fixed position on the Palestinians than by budgets, education, religious autonomy and military exemptions.

facts.text: The Israel Democracy Institute's Israeli Democracy Index 2022 says that on economic issues, and in several other areas, the differences between the political camps in Israel are small; a 2026 Al Jazeera analysis says economic and social policy cut across the camps rather than define them.

sources.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022
sources.quote: on economic issues, for example, and in several other areas, the differences between the political camps in Israel are small

sources.title: What 'right' and 'left' mean in Israel today
sources.quote: Economic and social policy still matter, but they often cut across the camps rather than defining them.

facts.text: The Israel Democracy Institute's Israeli Democracy Index 2022 reported that 62% of Israeli Jews placed themselves on the right, 24% in the centre and 11% on the left (multi-year average for the right: 49.5%).

sources.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022
sources.quote: In fact, today the Right (at 62%) is almost twice the size of the Center (24%) and Left (11%) combined

sources.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022
sources.quote: the Jewish public in Israel identifies largely with the Right (multiyear average, 49.5%)

sources.publisher: Israel Votes (election explainer, no named author)
sources.title: The American lens
sources.quote: Israeli Jews have also moved right on their own placement: 62% put themselves on the right in 2022, up from 46% in 2019.

facts.text: Pew Research Center's 2025 survey of Israelis reported that 54% of those on the left, 29% of those in the centre and 7% of those on the right said a way can be found for Israel and a Palestinian state to coexist.

sources.title: Potential for Israeli-Palestinian peace: Israeli public opinion
sources.quote: (54%) say a way can be found for Israel and a Palestinian state to coexist, compared with 29% of Israelis in the center and 7% of those on the right.

sources.publisher: Israel Votes (election explainer, no named author; second-hand report of the Pew survey)
sources.title: The American lens
sources.quote: In spring 2025, 54% of Israelis on the left and 7% on the right thought Israel and an independent Palestinian state could coexist peacefully

facts.text: Pew Research Center's 2025 survey of Israelis reported that four in ten Israeli Arabs think peaceful coexistence with a Palestinian state is possible, against 16% of Israeli Jews.

sources.title: Potential for Israeli-Palestinian peace: Israeli public opinion
sources.quote: Four-in-ten Israeli Arabs think peaceful coexistence is possible - more than double the 16% of Israeli Jews who say the same.

sources.title: Only 21% Israelis think peace with a Palestinian state is possible
sources.quote: Among Jewish Israelis, the results are even more stark: only 16% believe peaceful coexistence is achievable.

facts.text: The Israel Democracy Institute's Israeli Democracy Index 2022 treats the Arab public as a separate political camp, outside the right-left scale used for Jews, and an IDI analysis says many Arabs see themselves as identified with the left.

sources.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022
sources.quote: the Arab public, which does not identify with this fundamental Jewish Israeli ethos, to constitute a separate political camp.

sources.title: Jewish Israeli Voters Moving Right - Analysis
sources.quote: many Arabs see themselves as identified with the left.

sources.title: What 'right' and 'left' mean in Israel today
sources.quote: Parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel sit even further outside the Zionist right-left map.

facts.text: The Israel Democracy Institute's 2024 Israeli Democracy Index reported that 48% of respondents named the tension between the political Right and Left as the primary tension in Israeli society, a sharp increase; the Jerusalem Post's report on the 2025 Index says nearly half of respondents again named it the most serious social division.

sources.title: The Israel Democracy Institute Publishes its 2024 Israeli Democracy Index
sources.quote: This year, there was a sharp increase in the percentage of respondents who view the primary tension in Israeli society as being between the political Right and Left (48%).

sources.title: Israelis still believe in the country, but not its institutions, IDI survey reveals
sources.quote: nearly half of the respondents believe the most serious social division in Israel today is the divide between the political right and left

facts.text: Pew Research Center's 2024 survey reported that 19% of Israeli Jews thought peaceful coexistence with a Palestinian state is possible, down from 32% in 2023.

sources.title: How Israelis view societal conflicts and peaceful coexistence
sources.quote: Today, 19% of Jews think peaceful coexistence is possible, down from 32% who said the same in 2023

sources.title: After Oct. 7, just 19% of Israeli Jews believe a Palestinian state can peacefully coexist with Israel
sources.quote: It is down from 32% in a survey released just weeks before the war broke out.

facts.text: In America, party differences run across many issues: the size and role of government, the economy, immigration and race, and social questions such as abortion.

sources.title: How the political typology groups view major issues
sources.quote: there are wide differences between Republicans and Democrats, but relatively modest differences within each partisan coalition.

sources.title: Update: Partisan Gaps Expand Most on Government Power, Climate
sources.quote: Democrats' views that abortion should be legal under any circumstance increased significantly this year compared with 10 and 20 years earlier

sources.title: How the political typology groups view major issues
sources.quote: Opinions on immigration - like views on race - are mostly divided along partisan lines, though there also are differences within the coalitions.

facts.text: Gallup's 2025 survey of Americans reported that 76% of Democrats, 53% of independents and 41% of Republicans favour establishing an independent Palestinian state (a different question from the one Pew asked Israelis).

sources.title: Less Than Half in U.S. Now Sympathetic Toward Israelis
sources.quote: About three-quarters of Democrats, 76%, are in favor of such a state, compared with 53% of independents. While 41% of Republicans support a Palestinian state, 49% are opposed.

sources.title: American Support for Israel Hits Record Low
sources.quote: Around 76 percent of Democrats, 53 percent of independents and 41 percent of Republicans support an independent Palestinian state.

contested.text: How far the American parallel holds. The IDI says the Israeli divide now looks like Democrats against Republicans; a 2026 analysis says the terms no longer describe two mirror camps, and scholars still find party positions structured first by the conflict.

sources.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022
sources.quote: today the division between the two camps is more reminiscent of that between the Democrats and the Republicans in the United States.

sources.title: What 'right' and 'left' mean in Israel today
sources.quote: The Israeli left and right still exist. But the terms no longer describe two mirror camps competing over the same list of questions.

sources.title: The ideas of Israel
sources.quote: rather than sitting on any traditional left-right axis, these camps cut across three ideological axes: economic, security and identity.

contested.text: Whether the economy matters as little as the scholarly literature says: the IDI finds small economic differences between the camps, while an IDI survey summarised on an election explainer found Jewish respondents naming the economy and cost of living nearly as often as foreign affairs and security.

sources.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022
sources.quote: on economic issues, for example, and in several other areas, the differences between the political camps in Israel are small

sources.publisher: Israel Votes (election explainer, no named author)
sources.title: The American lens
sources.quote: Jewish respondents chose foreign affairs and security (39%), the economy and cost of living (38%) and conscription (27%).

could_not_verify: Two reliable sites besides the IDI that report the IDI Israeli Democracy Index 2022 statements (Democrats and Republicans; economic differences small; 62% / 24% / 11% self-placement). Searches found the IDI's own press release (same site), JNS and Jewish Press pieces without these figures, an i24 piece the checker could not read, and Times of Israel and Channel 12 reports that blocked the checker. A person would need to read an independent news or scholarly report of the 2022 Index.

Two reliable sites besides Pew that report Pew's 2025 left, centre and right figures (54%, 29%, 7%). JPost reports only that ideology shapes views; the Pew pages are one site. A person would need a news report quoting the ideology breakdown.

Two independent reports of the 40% against 16% Arab and Jewish figures (JPost has the 16%); of the IDI 2024 figure of 48%; and of Pew's 2024 figures of 19% and 32% (the IDI and Pew pages are one site each). The IDI 2024 and Pew 2024 facts rest on the record alone.
Two reliable sites besides the IDI for the IDI analysis that many Arab citizens see themselves as identified with the left, and for the Index treating the Arab public as a separate camp.

A third independent source for the American party differences (Pew and Gallup are two sites; a scholarly or reference page on the parties' platforms would be the third). Britannica and Merriam-Webster pages blocked the checker.
IDI self-placement figures for 2023 to 2025, after 7 October: none found in a page the checker can read.

Zur and Bakker (Party Politics, 2023), the study that places party positions first on the conflict, then culture, then the economy: the SAGE page blocks the checker; the claim rests on the IDI, Al Jazeera and ECFR pages.

A second Gallup reporter beyond Newsweek for the 2025 figures: the Anadolu, Yahoo and Ynet pages found report the 2026 poll or sympathy figures, not the 2025 statehood question. Pew's 2022 and 2024 US surveys on the best outcome could not be read by the checker.

Pew's 2016 Israel survey (86% of the left, 46% of the centre, 29% of the right) was removed from the Pew 2025 fact because it is a different record; a person who wants the trend would add it as its own record fact with two reporters.

Removed by the reviewer: the undated IDI 'Doves and Hawks' 52/26/22 figures from the self-placement fact (a different survey of a different population; one IDI article). The Avishai New Yorker clause stays in fact 1 as an attributed opinion; it is not a reader of the IDI Index and does not confirm it.
not_claimed: That Israeli and American politics are unrelated: the IDI itself sees a growing resemblance.
That Israeli voters ignore the economy, religion or identity.
That any one party or camp is right about the conflict.
That the worked example is a real person or a forecast.
That Pew and Gallup measure the same thing: Pew asks whether a way can be found for Israel and a Palestinian state to coexist; Gallup asks whether people favour establishing a Palestinian state.

answer_claims.says: In Israel, the Israel Democracy Institute and other sources describe left and right as defined mainly by one's stance on the conflict (territory, a Palestinian state, security), with religion and state a second line of division and small differences between the camps on economic issues.
In America the parties divide across many issues: government, economy, immigration, race, abortion.
The Institute's 2022 index says the Israeli divide is now more reminiscent of Democrats against Republicans, across a range of issues.
Pew's 2025 Israeli survey found 54% of the left, 29% of the centre and 7% of the right saying a way can be found for Israel and a Palestinian state to coexist.
Gallup's 2025 US survey, asking a different question, found 76% of Democrats and 41% of Republicans favouring an independent Palestinian state.

skeptic.notes: Read the cited pages with fetch; every quote is on its page and in context (IDI 2022 Index pdf, Pew 2025, Gallup 2025, ECFR, Al Jazeera, Pew 2016). Seat-free card; numbers are survey results, labelled with who asked. must-fix: 11 of 12 facts (1, 3-11, with fact 1's only second site a writer's opinion) fail the record rule: the IDI/Pew/Gallup record is opened, but there are not two independent readers. Where a second source exists it reports a different record (JPost 2025 Index against the IDI 2024 fact; Al Jazeera 2026 analysis against the IDI 2022 economics statement) or is second-hand with no named author (Israel Votes, kind other). The gate rightly refuses them. should-fix: fact 8 joins the IDI 2024 figure to a JPost report of the 2025 Index (a different record); fact 3 joins an IDI statement to an Al Jazeera analysis. should-fix: the 2022 Index's 62% 'right' is Jewish respondents only and a post-October-2023 figure is missing; the Israel Votes page notes a JPPI figure of 66% in July 2026 on a different scale (not carried). Strongest objection, from the Israeli political scientist: the card quotes the IDI's 'Democrats and Republicans' sentence, but the same Index says Arab citizens are a separate camp outside the scale, so the American parallel is for Jewish Israelis only; fact 7 carries this but the answer does not. From the critic of a Jewish state: the Israeli left/right axis excludes Arab citizens by construction (fact 7), which the card states but does not weigh. Fixed by me: labelled the New Yorker source in fact 1 as a writer's opinion that does not confirm the IDI record; removed the undated 'Doves and Hawks' figures from fact 4; added wire JTA to the Forward copy (fact 9).

citer.notes: Split into 5 claims, each tied to facts. Reworded: 'The labels sound alike but sort different things' removed (our verdict, no fact says it); 'The overlap is real in one respect' reworded to what the IDI says; 'Different questions, same direction' removed (our reading, and the two surveys ask different questions); 'economics weakest' reworded to the IDI's 'differences ... small'. must-fix: the answer's survey sentences rest on facts 5 and 11, which fail the record rule (one reader each at most); the card cannot be verified until independent reports are added.
